Set $E_1=\widehat{k_p}$, $E_2=\widehat{\mathbf a_p}$ and $E_3=E_1	imes E_2$; $B_{ij}=E_i\cdot BE_j$. Physical derivatives are relative to $I$; for interval $I$, endpoint derivatives are one-sided. Put $\sigma=|k_p(t_0)||\mathbf a_p(t_0)|$, $
u=B_{12}(t_0)>0$, $\eta=B_{32}(t_0)>0$, $r=\sqrt{2\sigma
u}$, $S=\sigma/r$, $\varepsilon=\eta/
u$, and $\delta=\sup_I|B_{12}/
u-1|+\sup_I|B_{32}/\eta-1|+\sup_I\|B\|/r+\sup_I\|E_c\|/
u$. Assume $T\ge2$ and $C_0\varepsilon\le1$, $C_0T^{C_0}\delta\le\varepsilon$ for sufficiently large integer $C_0$. In physical time, the new wave solves $k'=-M^Tk$, $\mathbf a'=-M\mathbf a+2(k\cdot M\mathbf a)k/|k|^2$, $k\cdot\mathbf a=0$, with $M=B+\mathbf a_p\otimes k_p+E_c$, $k(t_0)=\lambda E_3(t_0)$, $\lambda>0$, and $\mathbf a(t_0)=-E_1(t_0)/S+E_2(t_0)$. Use $	au=r(t-t_0)$ and $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon	au^2/2)$. Here a reference slope means any solution of $Y\prime=\cos^2\varphi(1-\varepsilon	an\varphi)-\varepsilon	au\sin2\varphi\,Y-Y^2$, $Y(0)=1$, on $[0,\infty)$. Such a solution is used to characterize the output $	au_m$; it is not a supplied input to the proposition. Define $E_{1,+}=k/|k|$, $E_{2,+}=\mathbf a/|\mathbf a|$, $E_{3,+}=E_{1,+}	imes E_{2,+}$, $
u_+=E_{1,+}\cdot ME_{2,+}$ and $\eta_+=E_{3,+}\cdot ME_{2,+}$. Assume $0<\varepsilon_+\le\varepsilon/32$ and $H=2/\sqrt{\varepsilon\varepsilon_+}\le T$. The formal statement identifies the unique nonnegative zero $	au_m$ of every reference slope, with $	au_m\ge2/\varepsilon$, and supplies a crossing $\eta_+/
u_+=\varepsilon_+$ in $[	au_m,H]$. It chooses one attained maximum $A=\max_{[0,T]}|\mathbf a|$. At every crossing in that interval, $\exp(-1)/(4\sqrt{\varepsilon\varepsilon_+})\le|\mathbf a||k|/(\lambda A)\le18\exp(3)/\sqrt{\varepsilon\varepsilon_+}$. On $[0,1]$ it gives $|\mathbf a|\le\exp(3-1/\sqrt\varepsilon)A$. These retain Proposition 2.8 with explicit absolute strength factors and the same early-time factor. Continuous $B$ and a larger compact observation set are permitted, with $\delta$ measured on that set. The proposition does not state uniqueness of a crossing or locate the perturbed amplitude maximum at $	au_m$. A separate older formal theorem locates a crossing strictly inside the bracket and uses the weaker symmetric lower factor $1/(18\exp(3))$; that is not the exact lower constant of the current formal statement. The universal integer threshold for $C_0$ is chosen before all physical wave data. Here hats denote division by Euclidean length.

statements.markdown:
We call a time $	au$ at which $\eta_+/
u_+=\varepsilon_+$ a *crossing*: there the ratio reaches the threshold $\varepsilon_+$ prescribed for the next wave. The next wave is activated at a crossing. The reference amplitude decreases after $	au_m$, and the wave-vector length is comparable to $\lambda/\cos\varphi$. The next proposition bounds their product for the actual wave at a crossing, and shows that its amplitude is small compared with its maximum during the first unit of normalized time. The strength $\sigma_+=|\mathbf a||k|$ at the crossing and the coupling $
u_+$ supply the frozen parameters $\sigma,
u$ for the next wave.
